title: How to Plan for Retirement When You’re Self-Employed or a Freelancer
description: Structuring your own 'Pension Plan' without an employer match.
content:
Self-employed Americans have the freedom of being their own boss, but the burden of being their own benefits department. You don't get a 401(k) match, you pay extra taxes (15.3% SE Tax), and your income is volatile. However, the tax code offers massive advantages to the self-employed—specifically the **Solo 401(k)** and **SEP IRA**—that allow you to save far more than W-2 employees ($69,000+ per year). This guide explains how to build a retirement fortress on a variable income.

Key Takeaways

  • The Solo 401(k) Superpower: This is the best account for solopreneurs. You can contribute as both employee ($23k) and employer (20-25% of profit). It allows for massive tax deductions.
  • Variable Contribution Strategy: Unlike a fixed paycheck deduction, you should save based on 'Feast and Famine.' In good months, sweep 30-40% of profit to retirement. In bad months, save 0%.
  • Automated Tax Drag: You must save for the IRS first. Always set aside 25-30% of every invoice for taxes. Do not invest your tax liability money.
  • Diversification: Your business is a 'Concentrated Asset.' Do not reinvest 100% of profits back into the business. Siphon cash out into the S&P 500 to diversify your risk.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Self-employed individuals can deduct health insurance premiums and HSA contributions directly from gross income. Stacking a Solo 401(k) + HSA allows you to shelter huge amounts of income from the highest tax brackets.

Solo 401(k) vs. SEP IRA

Choose your vehicle carefully.

Solo 401(k) (The Winner)

  • Contribution Limit: Up to $69,000 (2025).
  • Catch-Up: Yes ($7,500 if 50+).
  • Roth Option: Yes.
  • Loans: Yes (Borrow up to $50k).
  • Requirement: No employees (except spouse).

SEP IRA (The Runner Up)

  • Contribution Limit: Up to $69,000 (25% of comp).
  • Catch-Up: No.
  • Roth Option: Historically No (New rules allow it, but few custodians offer it yet).
  • Pros: Easier paperwork. Can set up after year-end (until tax day).

Verdict: Use the Solo 401(k) if you have no employees. It allows for higher contributions at lower income levels.

The 'Profit First' Retirement Flow

  1. Open Business Checking: Never mix personal and business funds. Revenue hits Business Checking.
  2. The 'Tax & Save' Transfer: Every Friday, transfer 30% to Tax Savings and 10% to Retirement Savings. Do it before paying yourself a salary.
  3. The Quarterly Dump: Once a quarter, move the Retirement Savings pile into your Solo 401(k) or SEP IRA. Invest it in a Target Date Fund.
  4. Roth vs. Pre-Tax: If you are in a 'startup' phase with low income, use the Roth Solo 401(k). Pay low taxes now. If you are 'crushing it' ($200k+ income), use Pre-Tax to lower your bill.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I open a Solo 401(k) if I have a day job?

Yes! But the 'Employee' limit ($23k) is shared across all jobs. If you max out at your day job, your side hustle Solo 401(k) can only receive 'Employer' profit-sharing contributions.

Do I need an EIN?

Yes. It is free from the IRS website. You need it to open a Solo 401(k).

Is my business sellable?

Most freelance businesses are not sellable. Do not count on 'Selling the Business' as your retirement plan. You need liquid assets (Stocks/Bonds) to retire.
